source_caption:
The Imitation Game tells the story of Alan Turing, but the real story behind it is even more complicated.

During World War II, Turing worked at Bletchley Park, where he played a crucial role in breaking Nazi Germany’s Enigma codes. He helped design the Bombe, a machine that dramatically accelerated the search for Enigma settings and became an important part of the Allied codebreaking effort. His work, along with that of many other mathematicians, linguists, engineers and intelligence workers, helped shorten the war and save countless lives.

The 2014 film, starring Benedict Cumberbatch, captures Turing’s brilliance and the immense pressure surrounding the work, but it changes quite a lot for dramatic effect. Turing didn’t single-handedly crack Enigma, and the film’s portrayal of him as a completely isolated genius is exaggerated. His relationship with Joan Clarke was also more complicated than the movie suggests. They were close colleagues and friends, and Turing did propose to her, but their relationship was not the central romantic story shown on screen.

The most heartbreaking part of Turing’s real life came after the war. In 1952, he was prosecuted for homosexual acts, which were then illegal in Britain. He was given the choice between imprisonment and chemical castration and chose the latter.

Just two years later, in 1954, Turing died at the age of 41.

For decades, much of his wartime work remained secret. Today, Alan Turing is remembered not only as one of the most important codebreakers of World War II, but also as a pioneering figure in computer science.

The movie tells a powerful story. The real one is even more tragic.

source_details.synopsis: The Imitation Game is a 2014 American biographical thriller film directed by Morten Tyldum and written by Graham Moore, based on the 1983 biography Alan Turing: The Enigma by Andrew Hodges. The film's title quotes the name of the game cryptanalyst Alan Turing proposed for answering the question "Can machines think?", in his 1950 seminal paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence". The film stars Benedict Cumberbatch as Turing, who devised new methods for decrypting German intelligence messages for the British government during World War II.
